opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I really like it. I think a lot of people, when they first try pair programming, find it a bit uncomfortable, because you're used to coding alone, where nobody sees your mistakes or the five times you Google the same thing. Having someone watch you work feels exposed at first.

Once you get past that, I find it really valuable. One big thing is that you just learn a ton. Everyone has their own little tricks: keyboard shortcuts, how they navigate a codebase, how they debug, what they check first when something breaks. You'd never learn those from reading someone's code, because the finished code doesn't show the process. Sitting next to someone, you pick them up constantly.

It also keeps you focused. When you're coding alone, it's easy to drift off and check Slack, or go down a rabbit hole that doesn't matter. When someone else is there, you both stay on task, and if one of you is heading down a dead end, the other one usually notices pretty quickly and says, "Wait, why are we doing this?"

And for the kind of work we do, where a lot of it is debugging large, complicated systems, two people looking at the same problem often catch things one person would miss. One person is driving and thinking about the immediate line of code, and the other can step back and think about the bigger picture.

The costs are real. It's tiring, and it's not always the most efficient use of two people's time, especially for routine tasks. So I don't think everything should be pair programmed. But for tricky problems, for onboarding someone new, or for spreading knowledge across a team, I think it's underrated. Some of the times I've learned the most have been sitting with someone more experienced and watching how they actually work.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses initial discomfort with being watched while pair programming, but does not say Nick Joseph was too nervous to take a bathroom break.

fable-5.1.text:
Nick Joseph: I actually love it. I think it's probably my favorite way to work, and it's funny because when I started out I was pretty skeptical of it. It felt like you were taking two people and getting one person's worth of output.

But in practice I think that's just wrong, at least for the kind of work we do. A lot of the time when you're working on something like a training run or debugging some weird behavior in the model, the hard part isn't typing. The hard part is figuring out what's going on, deciding what experiment to run next, noticing that the thing you assumed was true actually isn't. And having a second person there means you catch mistakes way faster. One of you is typing and the other is sort of watching and going, "Wait, didn't that variable get overwritten three lines ago?" That saves you an enormous amount of time compared to finding it two hours later when your run has already crashed.

The other thing is it's just a really good way to transfer knowledge. When someone new joins, the fastest way for them to pick up how the codebase works, what the gotchas are, how we think about things, is to sit next to someone and work through a real problem together. You pick up all this tacit stuff that never makes it into documentation. And it goes both ways: I've learned a lot from pairing with people who are much newer than me, because they ask questions about things I'd stopped thinking about, and sometimes the answer is "Actually, I don't know why we do it that way."

It also keeps you honest. It's much harder to go down a rabbit hole for three hours when there's someone else there who can say, "Is this actually the thing we're trying to solve?" I find I'm more focused and I get less stuck.

I'll say it's not perfect for everything. Some tasks are really just grinding through a bunch of boilerplate, and there you probably don't need two people. And it can be tiring; you're kind of "on" the whole time in a way you're not when you're working alone. But on net, if I had to pick one habit that's made me more productive as an engineer, it'd be that.

r001.rationale: The response discusses benefits and drawbacks of pair programming, but it does not say Nick felt too nervous to take a bathroom break.

astra-6.text:
I find it pretty enjoyable. Programming on your own, you can get stuck on something and spend a long time going down the wrong path. With another person there, you get that feedback much faster. And often just explaining what you’re trying to do helps you see the problem more clearly.

It can also be quite intense. You’re communicating all the time, and you have to find a rhythm that works for both people. So I wouldn’t want to do it all day, but for working through a tricky problem together, I really like it.
